verses.note: Christians have read the command in different ways: as forbidding all use of force (Anabaptists, Mennonites, and many early Christian writers), as governing personal relations but not the magistrate's duty to restrain evil (Augustine, Luther's two kingdoms, and the Reformed tradition, citing Romans 13:4), or as calling for active nonviolent resistance (Wink, Martin Luther King Jr.). All agree it forbids personal revenge.

Jesus acknowledges a legitimate sphere of civil authority, as Paul does in Romans 13:1-7, while placing it under God. Christians have developed the saying in different ways: Augustine's two cities, Luther's two kingdoms, and the Reformed and Catholic traditions of the state as God's servant under his law. None of them reads the verse as giving Caesar a realm where God's claim does not reach.

The Roman state holds the power of the sword, and the accusers must go through it. John shows both powers, religious and political, cooperating in an unjust death, and neither can escape responsibility by pointing to the other.

Jesus neither denies Pilate's authority nor bows to Rome's definition of rule. The verse has been cited on every side of Christian debates over church and state: by Augustine and Calvin to distinguish the spiritual kingdom from civil government, and by Anabaptist and Mennonite writers in refusing the sword. Its own point is that Christ's kingdom does not advance by coercion.

Political authority is real and derived. Pilate's power to release or crucify is given from above, which both limits it and makes him answerable for its use. Paul's teaching that the authorities are instituted by God (Romans 13:1) has here its sober counterpart: God-given authority can be used to condemn the innocent, and it is not excused for that.
Pilate's fear of Caesar outweighs his judgment that Jesus is innocent. The verse shows how political power, even when it recognizes the right, can be pushed into injustice by fear of losing position.

The authorities' request combines Roman procedure and Jewish law. Even in executing, the state is bound by a higher command about the dignity of the dead, and John notes how that command shaped the end of the day.

Paul wrote that the governing authorities are instituted by God (Romans 13:1); here a state receives its authority from the dragon. The two chapters are not in contradiction: a government that serves justice acts as God's servant, and one that demands worship and makes war on the saints has become the dragon's instrument. Oscar Cullmann, in The State in the New Testament (1956), set the two texts side by side as the New Testament's two faces of the state.
